title: Hardware multiplier (shift-and-add, Booth, Wallace tree)
summary: A hardware multiplier computes the product of two n-bit integers. Methods: shift-and-add (O(n^2) gate delay), Booth's algorithm (handles signed, reduces partial products), Wallace tree (parallel reduction of partial products, O(log n) delay), Dadda tree (similar, fewer gates). Modern CPUs use modified Booth encoding + Wallace/Dadda tree + carry-propagate adder.

structure.meaning: n partial products, each shifted by its position. E.g., for 4-bit: 4 partial products of 4 bits.
Iterative: if multiplier bit is 1, add multiplicand to accumulator; shift right. O(n) cycles.
Encodes pairs of multiplier bits: 00/11 -> 0, 01 -> +multiplicand, 10 -> -multiplicand. Reduces partial products for signed multiplication.
Encodes triples of multiplier bits. Fewer partial products (n/2 instead of n). Most common in modern CPUs.
Parallel reduction: 3:2 compressors (full adders) reduce partial products in a tree structure. Fast but area-intensive.
Similar to Wallace but minimizes the number of adders. Slightly slower but smaller.
Product of two n-bit integers is 2n bits.

notes: Multiplication is the most expensive integer operation (tens of cycles).
Modern CPUs use modified Booth encoding + Wallace tree + carry-propagate adder.
Fused multiply-add (FMA) computes (a*b)+c in one instruction with single rounding.
Floating-point multiplication uses mantissa multiplication + exponent addition.
SIMD multipliers operate on multiple elements in parallel.
